text.p: Zastava Group, Yugoslavia's biggest industrial enterprise, said the year 1997 would be crucial for the group.
"We have reached a point at which the group will either turn to positive trends or take another nose dive," said Srboljub Vasovic, Zastava's chief executive.

"Zastava is an exhausted system and there is no space for development or profit-making," Vasovic said in an interview with Reuters. "Without a significant financial injection Zastava will not recover."
The group, like the country's economy, was devastated by the violent break-up of former Yugoslavia in 1991, loss of markets, lack of funds, mismanagement and four years of U.N. sanctions.
The group needs radical reforms to recover, analysts interviewed by Reuters agreed. They said a change in ownership structure as well as financial help from abroad were vital.
The group restarted production in 1996 with government help but financial results have been weak.

The Zastava car factory, the biggest unit in the group, increased output to about 10,000 vehicles last year, up 30 percent on 1995. But that was a far cry from the pre-war annual output of 200,000 cars.

The budgeted 30,000 vehicle output in 1997 is deemed by many to be too optimistic. An insider, who asked not to be named, said it would be very difficult and even impossible to meet the target without an infusion of foreign funds.

Despite the small export deals struck with Macedonia and Egypt last year, the factory will have to overhaul both the engine and the body of its latest model launched in 1988 in case it is to return to the world market, analysts said.
Zastava, maker of the Yugo car, has been reported to be in talks with several potential partners, including Fiat, Renault and Toyota Motor Corp.
"Cooperation with a foreign partner is the only solution," Vasovic said, adding that the management had opted for an economic way out instead of a "slow death".
"We are very close but at the same time very far away from choosing our future partner," he said. "I expect the agreement soon. That is how things stand now....But the situation can quickly change."
According to Vasovic, ownership transformation would speed up Zastava's negotiations with potential foreign partners.
"We are prepared to offer foreign investors a controlling stake and give them management control but the price must be real and production must continue," he said.
Zastava, whose production line also includes trucks, weaponry and machine tools, has more than 13,000 workers on the payroll in its car plant, out of the about 40,000 employed.
Some analysts argue that at least half of the workers are superfluous and that fear of social unrest in case of drastic labour cuts is delaying the talks with possible foreign partners.
Vasovic rejected claims that the number of workers in the plants was obstructing the talks. He said he was aware drastic measures had to be taken to restructure and modernise the ailing enterprise.
The Belgrade-based Economics institute is commissioned to outline a privatisation programme for the Zastava group and the restructuring of personnel of the car factory by the end of January.
But Vasovic said both the international and domestic environments were unfavourable for Zastava at present.

The U.N. sanctions were lifted last year, but the so-called "outer wall" of sanctions remained in place preventing Yugoslavia's access to international funds and were burdening the negotiations with possible foreign partners.
A two-month-long citizens' protest in Serbia over local election fraud were also slowing down the talks.
-- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom ++381 11 222 4254
